patient.name: Gloria Bailey
patient.complaint: Red, hot, painful left lower leg for 2 days
background: Cracked skin and athlete's foot between her left toes
Says she is 'allergic' to amoxicillin: it gave her diarrhoea

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a unilateral red, hot, swollen, tender lower leg and fever, against DVT, gout and thrombophlebitis; or questions on the organism, Eron class and necrotising fasciitis.

points: Gloria, 61, noticed her left shin turning **red and hot** 2 days ago.
It is swollen, sore to touch and spreading.
She feels shivery and generally unwell (**malaise**).

steps.lead: A one-sided red, hot lower leg in a febrile woman: an **acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue**.
Gloria has almost every risk factor: **obesity**, **oedema**, **diabetes** and **breaks in the skin** from athlete's foot.

points: Exam: **poorly defined** erythema from ankle to mid-shin, warm and tender.
Faint **red streaks** run up the inner thigh.
Cracked, macerated skin between the 4th and 5th toes.
Calf soft; no blistering, no crepitus; foot pulses present.

steps.lead: Gloria's red streaks are **lymphangitis**. The likely organism is **Streptococcus pyogenes**, then Staphylococcus aureus.

steps.title: Red, swollen leg: cellulitis or something else?
head: Feature
Cellulitis
DVT
Gout

steps.q: Gloria has a hot, red, tender shin with fever and red streaks. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Unilateral red, warm, tender skin with **fever** and **lymphangitis** is cellulitis. DVT and eczema do not cause fever and red streaks.

steps.lead: Gloria is systemically well (mild fever, normal BP and HR under 100) but has **diabetes and obesity**: **Eron Class IIa**.

visual.title: Eron class: where is Gloria?
visual.label: Gloria IIa
visual.caption: Class I and IIa: oral treatment usually fine. IIb and above: admit and consider IV antibiotics. **Class IV** = sepsis or necrotising fasciitis.

steps.lead: Gloria is **diabetic**, so watch for spread to **necrotising fasciitis** or **sepsis**: pain out of proportion, crepitus, dusky skin or falling BP.

steps.text: Cellulitis is usually **unilateral**. Two red, swollen legs are more likely venous eczema or lipodermatosclerosis, not 'bilateral cellulitis'.
Classic stem: one red, hot, tender, swollen lower leg, **fever**, poorly defined erythema and a portal of entry (cut, bite, tinea). Answer: **cellulitis**.

investigation.exam: Expect a question on whether any test is needed (cellulitis is a **clinical diagnosis**), the expected blood results (raised CRP and WCC), or blood cultures in a systemically unwell patient.

steps.lead: Gloria's diagnosis is made from her history and the look of her leg. No scan or swab is needed to **confirm** it.

steps.q: What confirms that Gloria has cellulitis?
steps.r: Cellulitis is a **clinical diagnosis**. Blood tests support it; Doppler is only if you also suspect a DVT.

steps.title: Gloria's bloods
steps.text: Raised **CRP** and **WCC** fit a bacterial infection. High glucose: infection upsets diabetic control.

steps.lead: Gloria's **CRP** and **WCC** are raised. She is not severely unwell, so blood cultures are not needed now.

visual.title: Gloria's CRP
visual.label: Gloria 118
visual.caption: A raised CRP supports infection; repeat it if she is not improving.

steps.title: Which tests for which patient?
nodes: Yes: blood cultures before IV antibiotics

steps.text: A **skin swab** of intact skin is pointless. Blood cultures are for **severe** infection, not for every cellulitis.
If the stem asks how to **confirm** cellulitis, the answer is clinical diagnosis, not an imaging test.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' with oral flucloxacillin as the answer, then the twists: true penicillin allergy, pregnancy, cat bites (co-amoxiclav), sepsis (IV co-amoxiclav, vancomycin if MRSA).

points: Gloria says she is **allergic to amoxicillin**.
On questioning: it only gave her loose stools and nausea.
No rash, swelling or breathing problems.

steps.q: Is Gloria's reaction to amoxicillin a penicillin allergy?
o: No: diarrhoea and nausea are side effects
Yes: she needs a test dose
steps.r: Diarrhoea and nausea are **common side effects**, not allergy. She can safely take flucloxacillin.

steps.lead: So Gloria gets **oral flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS for 5–7 days**, with leg **elevation** and analgesia.
Had Gloria been truly allergic (e.g. rash or anaphylaxis), she would get **clarithromycin** or doxycycline; erythromycin if pregnant.

steps.title: Which antibiotic?
head: Situation
Antibiotic
rows: Cat bite / infected insect bite in diabetic
**IV co-amoxiclav** + IV fluids; IV vancomycin if MRSA

steps.lead: If Gloria became septic, she would need **IV co-amoxiclav** and IV fluids; a cat bite would mean **co-amoxiclav** for Pasteurella.

visual.title: Gloria on oral flucloxacillin
visual.caption: Fever settles and CRP falls. Redness may look worse in the first 48 hours before improving; draw round the edge to track it.

steps.lead: Gloria's care follows **NICE NG141** (cellulitis and erysipelas) and the **Eron classification** for deciding oral versus IV and admission.

steps.text: Do not label diarrhoea on amoxicillin as 'penicillin allergy'. It pushes patients onto worse, broader antibiotics.
Bite (cat, or infected insect bite in a diabetic) = **co-amoxiclav**. Septic = **IV**. MRSA = **vancomycin**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on the organism and how it gets in, why the skin is red, warm and swollen, why lymphangitis streaks, and why oedema, obesity and diabetes predispose.

steps.lead: Streptococci entered Gloria's skin through the cracks between her toes and set off an **acute inflammatory response** in the dermis.

steps.title: From a crack in the skin to a red, hot leg
nodes: Strep pyogenes or Staph aureus invade

steps.lead: Gloria's red streaks follow her **lymphatic channels** up the leg towards the inguinal nodes.
Gloria's ankle **oedema** and obesity slow lymph drainage and perfusion, so bacteria take hold and clear slowly.

steps.q: Why does Gloria's chronic ankle oedema make cellulitis more likely?
o: It impairs lymphatic drainage and local perfusion
It raises her white cell count
steps.r: Poor **lymphatic drainage** and perfusion predispose to bacterial invasion and slow recovery.

steps.lead: Because Gloria is **diabetic**, infection could spread deeper to the fascia (**necrotising fasciitis**) or into the blood (**sepsis**).

steps.text: Treat the **portal of entry** too: Gloria's athlete's foot needs an antifungal to stop recurrence.

mcq.q: Which layers of skin does cellulitis affect?
mcq.r: Cellulitis is an **acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue**.

mcq.q: What is the most common organism causing cellulitis?
mcq.r: **Strep pyogenes** is most common, followed by **Staph aureus**.

mcq.q: What does red streaking up the limb in cellulitis represent?
mcq.r: **Lymphangitis**: spread along lymphatics towards regional nodes.

mcq.q: Which Eron class is a patient who is systemically well but has a comorbidity?
mcq.r: **Class IIa**: systemically well with a comorbidity.

mcq.q: Which serious complication can untreated cellulitis progress to?
What is the first-line antibiotic for uncomplicated cellulitis?
o: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS for 5–7 days

mcq.q: Which antibiotic covers Pasteurella multocida after a cat bite?
mcq.r: Oral **co-amoxiclav** is first-line for cat bites.

mcq.q: What is given for a pregnant woman with cellulitis and penicillin allergy?
mcq.r: Oral **erythromycin**; doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy.

mcq.q: Why are oedema and obesity risk factors for cellulitis?
o: They impair lymphatic drainage and local perfusion
mcq.r: Impaired **perfusion and lymph drainage** predispose to invasion and slow resolution.

technique.stem: A 54 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful right lower leg after scratching it on a garden fence. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. The right shin is swollen, warm and tender with poorly defined erythema. The left leg is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A red-leg diagnosis question: infection, clot, crystal or skin?

clues: after scratching it on a garden fence
steps.x: Portal of entry, fever, unilateral red hot tender shin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: DVT gives calf swelling without fever, a skin break or spreading erythema.
Gout affects a joint, usually the big toe, not the shin.
Thrombophlebitis is a tender cord along a vein, without spreading erythema.
Venous eczema is itchy, scaly, often bilateral and without fever.

steps.x: **A. Cellulitis.** Unilateral, hot, red, tender + fever + skin break.

technique.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 3 day history of a red, hot, swollen left forearm after a cat scratch. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. There is poorly defined erythema with red streaks towards the elbow. Blood tests are sent.
technique.q: Which is the most likely finding on her blood tests?

steps.x: Predict the blood results in a bacterial skin infection.
Cellulitis with lymphangitis: an acute bacterial infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: A bacterial infection raises, not lowers, CRP and WCC.
Eosinophils rise in allergy and parasites, not cellulitis.
Low platelets are not a feature of simple cellulitis.
Uric acid is for gout.

steps.x: **C. Raised CRP and WCC.** Supports a clinical diagnosis.

technique.stem: A 39 year old man has cellulitis of his left lower leg. He is systemically well with no comorbidities. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. He says he is allergic to penicillin because amoxicillin once gave him diarrhoea and nausea. He has never had a rash or swelling.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: First-line antibiotic, but check the allergy story.

clues: amoxicillin once gave him diarrhoea and nausea
never had a rash or swelling
steps.x: Eron Class I; the 'allergy' is a side effect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Not a true allergy, so **oral flucloxacillin**.

elim: Clarithromycin is for true penicillin allergy.
Clindamycin is an allergy alternative, and causes C. difficile.
Erythromycin is for pregnant patients with true allergy.
IV vancomycin is for MRSA or sepsis.

steps.x: **D. Flucloxacillin.** Diarrhoea is a side effect, not an allergy.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman has a 2 day history of a red, warm, swollen, tender area on her right shin after an insect bite. Her temperature is 38.1°C. The area has poorly defined margins. There is no joint involvement and her calf is soft.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the redness, warmth and swelling?
o: Acute inflammatory response with vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
Deep vein clot obstructing venous return

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bacteria in the dermis trigger **acute inflammation**: vasodilation, leaky vessels, neutrophils.

elim: Clot causes swelling, not fever with spreading erythema; calf is soft.
Allergy gives itchy wheals, not fever.
No tumour; this is acute.
Urate crystals cause gout in a joint.

steps.x: **A. Acute inflammatory response.** Rubor, calor, tumor, dolor.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a 3 day history of a painful left lower leg. He has a cracked heel. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. The left shin is red, hot, swollen and tender with poorly defined margins.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Unilateral red, hot, tender shin with fever, raised inflammatory markers and a skin break is cellulitis. Necrotising fasciitis would give pain out of proportion and systemic toxicity.

steps.x: Most likely diagnosis for a red, hot leg.
Risk factor, portal of entry, fever, classic skin signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: DVT does not give fever with spreading red, hot skin.
Lipodermatosclerosis is chronic, woody and usually bilateral.
No crepitus, dusky skin or pain out of proportion; he is stable.
Venous eczema is itchy, scaly and afebrile.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has a 2 day history of a red, hot, tender area on her right calf that started around a small cut from shaving. Her temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. There is no pus and no history of animal bites, swimming or recent hospital stay.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Strep pyogenes is the most common cause of cellulitis, ahead of Staph aureus. Pasteurella follows animal bites; Pseudomonas follows water exposure.

clues: no history of animal bites, swimming or recent hospital stay
steps.x: Simple non-purulent cellulitis with no special exposure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: E. coli causes UTIs, not typical cellulitis.
Pasteurella needs a cat or dog bite.
Pseudomonas follows water exposure or burns.
Staph epidermidis is a skin commensal causing line infections.

steps.x: **E. Strep pyogenes.** Most common; Staph aureus second.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with type 2 diabetes and heart failure has cellulitis of his right lower leg. He feels well in himself. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 86 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He is alert and orientated.
practice.q: Which is the most likely Eron classification?
practice.e: Systemically well but with comorbidities (diabetes, heart failure) is Eron Class IIa. Class I needs no comorbidities; IIb needs systemic illness.

steps.x: Severity class: is he unwell, and does he have comorbidities?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Class I has no comorbidities.
IIb needs systemic illness.
III needs significant systemic upset or limb threat.
IV is sepsis or necrotising fasciitis.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with poorly controlled diabetes has had cellulitis of her left thigh for 2 days. Over 6 hours she develops severe pain far worse than the visible redness. The skin is now dusky with blisters and crepitus. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 132 bpm and BP 88/52 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication that has developed?
practice.e: Pain out of proportion, dusky blistering skin, crepitus and shock in a diabetic with cellulitis means spread to necrotising fasciitis (Eron Class IV). It needs urgent surgery.

steps.x: A complication of cellulitis in a diabetic.

clues: far worse than the visible redness
steps.x: Rapid spread, gas in tissue, shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Compartment syndrome follows trauma or fracture, without crepitus.
DVT does not cause crepitus or shock like this.
Erysipelas is superficial and well demarcated.
Osteomyelitis is slower and does not cause crepitus.

steps.x: **D. Necrotising fasciitis.** Pain out of proportion + crepitus.

practice.stem: A 28 year old man has a 2 day history of a red, hot, swollen right foot after stepping on a nail. He now has tender red lines running up the inside of his leg and a tender lump in his right groin. His temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the red lines on his leg?
practice.e: Red streaking towards tender regional nodes is lymphangitis: cellulitis spreading along superficial lymphatic channels.

clues: tender red lines running up the inside of his leg
tender lump in his right groin
steps.x: Spreading infection towards the inguinal nodes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Thrombophlebitis is a firm cord along a vein, without groin nodes.
Varicose veins are blue, not tender red lines.
Vasculitis gives purpura, not streaks to a node.
Eczema is scaly and itchy.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman with obesity and chronic leg oedema has a 2 day history of a painful left lower leg and malaise. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. The doctor examines the leg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the leg?
practice.e: Cellulitis gives poorly defined, warm, tender erythema, usually on one leg.

clues: painful left lower leg and malaise
steps.x: Risk factors plus fever and a painful leg: cellulitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cellulitis is unilateral and painful.
That is acute limb ischaemia.
That is psoriasis.
Target lesions are erythema multiforme.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man has a 2 day history of a red, hot, tender right shin after a grazed knee. He is systemically well. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. His calf is soft and non-tender and he has no DVT risk factors. The junior doctor asks which test will confirm the diagnosis.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Cellulitis is a clinical diagnosis made on history and examination. Bloods (CRP, WCC) support it; blood cultures are only for severe infection.

steps.x: Classic, mild cellulitis; nothing pointing to DVT or deep infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Blood cultures are for severe infection; he is well.
Doppler is for suspected DVT.
MRI is for suspected deep infection such as osteomyelitis.
Biopsy is never needed for simple cellulitis.

steps.x: **D. Clinical diagnosis.** History and examination alone.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman with diabetes has cellulitis of her right leg and is now drowsy. Her temperature is 39.3°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 90/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. IV antibiotics are about to be started.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation before antibiotics?
practice.e: In severe cellulitis or sepsis, take blood cultures before IV antibiotics. A swab of intact skin is useless.

steps.x: Test before antibiotics in a severely unwell patient.

clues: IV antibiotics are about to be started
steps.x: Systemically unwell: severe cellulitis with sepsis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: D-dimer is for VTE and is raised in infection anyway.
X-ray does not change immediate care.
Swabbing intact skin grows nothing useful.
Uric acid is for gout.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures.** Severe cellulitis = cultures, then IV antibiotics.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has a 2 day history of a red, hot, tender left lower leg. She has no allergies and no comorbidities and is not pregnant. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. She is eating and drinking normally.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Eron Class I cellulitis: oral flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS for 5–7 days with elevation and analgesia.

steps.x: Eron Class I; no reason to deviate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Clarithromycin is for penicillin allergy.
IV co-amoxiclav is for sepsis.
Topical treatment cannot reach the dermis.
Vancomycin is for MRSA.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with type 1 diabetes was bitten on the hand by his cat 2 days ago. The hand is now red, hot and swollen around the bite. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. He has no allergies.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
practice.e: Cat bites need oral co-amoxiclav to cover Pasteurella multocida. Flucloxacillin alone misses Pasteurella.

clues: bitten on the hand by his cat
red, hot and swollen around the bite
steps.x: Cat bite cellulitis in a diabetic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Clarithromycin is the allergy option, with poor Pasteurella cover alone.
Flucloxacillin does not cover Pasteurella.
Metronidazole alone covers only anaerobes.
Nitrofurantoin is for UTIs only.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant has a 2 day history of a red, hot, tender right lower leg. She had anaphylaxis to penicillin as a child. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. She is systemically well.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: In pregnancy with true penicillin allergy, oral erythromycin is used. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy; beta-lactams are unsafe after anaphylaxis.

steps.x: Antibiotic for cellulitis with two twists.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Clarithromycin is the non-pregnant allergy choice.
Co-amoxiclav is a penicillin: anaphylaxis risk.
Doxycycline stains fetal teeth and bone.
Flucloxacillin is a penicillin.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with obesity, chronic lymphoedema of both legs and peripheral vascular disease has his third episode of left leg cellulitis this year. Each episode resolves slowly. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his recurrent infection and slow resolution?
o: Impaired lymphatic drainage and local perfusion
Increased neutrophil numbers in the skin
practice.e: Oedema, obesity and vascular disease impair local perfusion and lymphatic drainage, predisposing to bacterial invasion and slowing resolution.

steps.x: All three impair blood or lymph flow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cellulitis is infective, not autoimmune.
More neutrophils would help, not hinder.
Gastric acid is irrelevant to skin.
Scurvy is not suggested.

prompts.q: What is cellulitis and where does it usually occur?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the layers and the typical site.

points.p: Acute bacterial infection
Of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue
Usually the lower limb, unilateral
points.why: Bilateral red legs are rarely cellulitis.

prompts.q: What are the risk factors for cellulitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: anything breaking the skin barrier or reducing perfusion.

points.p: Breaks in the skin (wounds, insect bites)
Obesity and oedema
Diabetes and peripheral vascular disease
Chronic skin changes
points.why: Tinea pedis is a common hidden entry point.

prompts.q: How does cellulitis present, and which organisms cause it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: signs plus the two organisms.

points.p: Red, hot, swollen, tender skin
Poorly defined erythema
Fever and malaise
Lymphangitis: red streaking
Strep pyogenes (most common) and Staph aureus

prompts.q: What is the Eron classification of cellulitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: well or unwell, comorbid or not.

points.p: Class I: no systemic illness, no comorbidities
Class IIa: systemically well with a comorbidity; IIb: unwell with comorbidities
Class III: significant systemic upset, unstable comorbidity or limb threat
Class IV: sepsis or necrotising fasciitis

prompts.q: What are the complications of cellulitis, and who is most at risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the deeper and the systemic spread.

points.p: Necrotising fasciitis
points.why: Pain out of proportion, crepitus: urgent surgery.

points.p: Bacteraemia and sepsis
Higher risk in immunocompromised or diabetic patients

prompts.q: How is cellulitis diagnosed and which tests help?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical first, bloods to support.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis on history and examination (gold standard)
Raised CRP and WCC
Blood cultures if severe infection suspected

prompts.q: What is the first-line treatment for cellulitis, with dose and duration?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: drug, dose, frequency, duration, supportive care.

points.p: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS
For 5–7 days
Or co-amoxiclav for broader cover
points.why: E.g. near the face or bites.

points.p: Elevation of the limb and analgesia

prompts.q: What do you give if the patient is penicillin allergic, or pregnant and allergic?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: is it a true allergy?

points.p: Clarithromycin, doxycycline or clindamycin
Pregnant with penicillin allergy: oral erythromycin
Diarrhoea or nausea on amoxicillin is a side effect, not allergy

prompts.q: How do you treat a cat bite, severe cellulitis and cellulitis with sepsis?

points.p: Cat bite (or infected insect bite in diabetic): oral co-amoxiclav
Severe: IV antibiotics (e.g. flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav, ceftriaxone) and urgent surgical review
Sepsis: IV co-amoxiclav and IV fluids
MRSA suspected or confirmed: IV vancomycin

prompts.q: Why does cellulitis make the skin red, warm and swollen, and why do red streaks appear?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: entry, invasion, inflammation, spread.

points.p: Bacteria breach the skin barrier and invade dermis and subcutaneous tissue
points.why: Via a wound, bite or chronic skin change.

points.p: Acute inflammation: vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, neutrophils
Lymphangitis: infection spreading along superficial lymphatics to regional nodes

prompts.q: Why do oedema, obesity and diabetes predispose to cellulitis and its spread?

points.p: Impaired local perfusion and lymphatic drainage
In diabetes or immunocompromise, infection extends deeper or into the blood

glossary.Cellulitis: Acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually of one lower leg.
glossary.Dermis: The layer of skin under the epidermis, containing vessels, nerves and lymphatics.
glossary.Subcutaneous tissue: The fatty layer beneath the dermis.
glossary.Erysipelas: Superficial form of cellulitis of the upper dermis with a sharp, raised edge.
glossary.Erythema: Redness of the skin from dilated blood vessels.
glossary.Lymphangitis: Inflammation of lymphatic vessels, seen as red streaks tracking towards lymph nodes.
glossary.Streptococcus pyogenes: Group A Strep; the most common cause of cellulitis.
glossary.Staphylococcus aureus: Gram-positive bacterium; the second commonest cause of cellulitis.
glossary.MRSA: Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; resistant to flucloxacillin, treated with vancomycin.
glossary.Pasteurella multocida: Bacterium from cat and dog mouths that infects bite wounds; covered by co-amoxiclav.
glossary.Eron classification: Grades cellulitis severity from Class I (well, no comorbidity) to Class IV (sepsis or necrotising fasciitis).
glossary.Necrotising fasciitis: Rapidly spreading, life-threatening infection of the fascia; pain out of proportion, crepitus, needs surgery.
glossary.Crepitus: Crackling felt under the skin from gas in the tissues.
glossary.Malaise: A general feeling of being unwell.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection.
glossary.Flucloxacillin: Narrow-spectrum penicillin active against Staph aureus and Strep; first-line for cellulitis.
glossary.Co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid; broader cover, used for bites and severe cellulitis.
glossary.Clarithromycin: Macrolide antibiotic used in penicillin allergy.
glossary.Erythromycin: Macrolide antibiotic; the choice for penicillin-allergic pregnant women.
glossary.Doxycycline: Tetracycline antibiotic; avoided in pregnancy and young children.
glossary.Clindamycin: Antibiotic for penicillin allergy; carries a high risk of C. difficile diarrhoea.
glossary.Vancomycin: IV glycopeptide antibiotic used for MRSA.
glossary.Penicillin allergy: True immune reaction to penicillin: rash, angioedema or anaphylaxis, not diarrhoea or nausea.
glossary.Tinea pedis: Athlete's foot: fungal infection between the toes, a common entry point for cellulitis.
glossary.Lymphoedema: Chronic swelling from poor lymphatic drainage.
glossary.Oedema: Swelling from excess fluid in the tissues.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: an inflammatory marker that rises in bacterial infection.
glossary.WCC: White cell count; raised in bacterial infection.
glossary.DVT: Deep vein thrombosis: clot in a deep leg vein causing calf swelling and pain.
glossary.Thrombophlebitis: Inflamed, clotted superficial vein felt as a tender cord.
glossary.Venous eczema: Itchy, scaly skin on the lower legs from chronic venous hypertension, often bilateral.
glossary.Lipodermatosclerosis: Chronic hardening and brown-red discolouration of lower-leg skin from venous disease.
glossary.Portal of entry: The break in the skin through which bacteria get in.
